newsitem.title: BELARUS: Russian TV says Belarus detains its second crew.
newsitem.headline: Russian TV says Belarus detains its second crew.

text.p: Belarus police detained a second television crew from Russia's ORT channel at the Belarus-Lithuanian border on Friday, an ORT spokesman said.

Dmitry Novozhilov of ORT's office in the Belarussian capital told Reuters the four-member crew had been detained by border guards in a replay of events on July 26, when another group was detained for illegally crossing the border.
No official confirmation of the detentions or comment on them was immediately available.
Appeals for the release of the first crew, two of whom could face five years in prison, have elicited little response from legal authorities in the former Soviet republic of 10 million people.

President Alexander Lukashenko and Russian President Boris Yeltsin exchanged harsh words over the original arrests, with Yeltsin threatening to review a union treaty signed this year on integration between the neighbouring former Soviet republics.

The second crew had intended to show that the Belarussian-Lithuanian border was not clearly defined and that the original arrests of correspondent Pavel Sheremet and his colleagues had been politically inspired.
"Pavel Sheremet has already shown that this border only exists on paper and the guys wanted to show this one more time," ORT correspondent Viktor Dyatlikovich said.
Lukashenko has constantly accused Russian media of portraying his leadership in a deliberately negative light.
He accused the ORT journalists of being in the pay of unnamed foreign powers and said he had no right to free them.
A European Union official in Minsk to mediate talks with the opposition recently said he had asked the president to free the crew but Lukashenko had noted it was a matter for the courts.

Russian television crews have been denied access to feed pictures to Moscow and Western officials and institutions have accused Minsk of placing stringent curbs on the media and other human rights violations.
Lukashenko's rule has become increasingly authoritarian, particularly since he vastly broadened his powers following a landslide win of a controversial referendum last November.
His policy of forming a union with Russia and nostalgia for the Soviet Union have brought him broad support at home, where he swept to power in a surprise election win in 1994.
